summary.text: For an even integer \(m=2N\), the two primes symmetric about \(N\) supplied by the hypothesis sum to \(m\); the finitely many cases \(2\le N\le6\) are handled by explicit prime decompositions. For odd \(n>7\), applying the hypothesis to the even center \(n-1\) gives a prime \(p\) and the prime \((n-1)-(2p-1)=n-2p\), hence \(n=(n-2p)+2p\), while \(7=3+2\cdot2\) handles the boundary case.

full_proof.text:
Let \(a(N)=A261627(N)\) be defined as follows. Set
\[
\varepsilon_N=\begin{cases}
1,&N\equiv 1\pmod 2,\\
2,&N\not\equiv 1\pmod 2.
\end{cases}
\]
For a prime \(p<N+1\), put
\[
k=p\varepsilon_N-1.
\]
Then \(a(N)\) is the number of such primes \(p\) for which
\[
k<N,\qquad N-k\text{ is prime},\qquad N+k\text{ is prime}.
\]
The condition \(k<N\) is important because all subtraction is in the natural numbers: it ensures that \(N-k\) is the ordinary, untruncated difference.

Assume the positivity conjecture for this sequence:
\[
 a(N)>0\qquad\text{for every }N>6.
\]
We prove both the strong Goldbach conjecture and Lemoine's conjecture.

First we prove Goldbach's conjecture. Let \(m\ge 4\) be even. Since \(m\) is even, there is a natural number \(N\) such that
\[
m=N+N=2N.
\]
Suppose first that \(N>6\). The assumed positivity gives \(a(N)>0\). Hence the finite set counted by \(a(N)\) is nonempty, so there is a prime \(p<N+1\) such that, with
\[
k=p\varepsilon_N-1,
\]
we have \(k<N\), and both
\[
r=N-k\quad\text{and}\quad s=N+k
\]
are prime. Because \(k<N\), the subtraction defining \(r\) is exact in the natural numbers. Consequently
\[
r+s=(N-k)+(N+k)=2N=m.
\]
Thus \(m\) is the sum of the two primes \(r\) and \(s\).

It remains to handle \(N\le 6\). The inequality \(m=2N\ge4\) implies \(N\ge2\), so only \(N=2,3,4,5,6\) can occur. In these five cases we have the explicit prime decompositions
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
N&m=2N&\text{prime decomposition}\\ \hline
2&4&4=2+2,\\
3&6&6=3+3,\\
4&8&8=3+5,\\
5&10&10=5+5,\\
6&12&12=5+7.
\end{array}
\]
Every even natural number at least \(4\) is therefore a sum of two primes. This is the strong Goldbach conjecture.

We next prove Lemoine's conjecture. Let \(n\ge7\) be odd. We must exhibit primes \(r,p\) such that
\[
n=r+2p.
\]
If \(n=7\), this follows immediately from
\[
7=3+2\cdot2,
\]
and both \(3\) and \(2\) are prime.

Now suppose \(n\ne7\). Since \(n\ge7\), this means \(n>7\). Set
\[
N=n-1.
\]
Then \(N>6\). Moreover, because \(n\) is odd, it can be written as \(n=2t+1\) for some natural number \(t\). Hence
\[
N=n-1=2t
\]
is even, so \(N\not\equiv1\pmod2\). Therefore the selector in the definition of \(a(N)\) is
\[
\varepsilon_N=2.
\]

By the assumed positivity conjecture, \(a(N)>0\). Thus there is at least one prime \(p<N+1\) counted by \(a(N)\). For this \(p\), since \(\varepsilon_N=2\), the associated displacement is
\[
k=2p-1.
\]
The defining conditions for being counted give
\[
2p-1<N,
\]
and say in particular that
\[
r=N-(2p-1)
\]
is prime. (They also say that \(N+(2p-1)\) is prime, although this second prime is not needed for Lemoine's conjecture.) Membership of \(p\) in the set of primes below \(N+1\) also tells us that \(p\) itself is prime.

It remains only to check the required identity. Since \(p\) is prime, \(p>0\), so \(2p-1\) is the ordinary predecessor of \(2p\). The bound \(2p-1<N\) ensures that the subtraction in the definition of \(r\) is untruncated. Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
r+2p
&=N-(2p-1)+2p\\
&=N+1\\
&=(n-1)+1\\
&=n.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus \(n=r+2p\), where both \(r\) and \(p\) are prime. This proves Lemoine's conjecture for every odd \(n\ge7\).

We have proved that the assertion \(a(N)>0\) for every \(N>6\) implies both the strong Goldbach conjecture and Lemoine's conjecture.
